cases.description: Every transaction type at once: both billed legs count, the reversal subtracts, the settlement is invisible.
success_fee is written -p_amount. Read through its own sign it is positive billed fee.
success_fee_arrears is written p_amount — POSITIVE, because it accrues a debt rather than moving the wallet. Opposite sign to the charge leg, same billed fee.
A reversal subtracts from net and leaves gross untouched. Under Math.abs over a billed set it would have added.
arrears_settlement moves an amount the arrears row already counted as billed. In gross it doubles the fee; in reversals it subtracts a fee nobody reversed.
Top-ups, boosts, subscriptions, refunds and disputes are not fee generation. They must not move any of the three figures.
A success_fee written POSITIVE contradicts the live function's -p_amount. Unavailable, never normalised: Math.abs read this as 30.
A fee_reversal written negative contradicts reverse_success_fee's v_fee_amount. All three unavailable under the all-or-nothing ruling.
Neither RPC can write a zero fee. A row that says otherwise is unexpected, not an absent fee.
verify_redemption commits status='success' before the fee step and swallows its exception, so a genuine success can carry no ledger row at all. The total is unknown, not smaller.
Nothing happened. That is an ANSWER, and it is zero — not unavailable. Confusing the two is how a quiet period reads as a broken read.
D188: the redemption itself is demo-tagged. Its fee never reaches an executive figure.
D188: the parent merchant is demo-tagged. The ledger row itself carries nothing about its merchant, which is why this is a join and not a column read.
D188, the live production shape: a non-demo merchant holding a demo deal, and claim_deal never sets redemptions.is_demo.
The window is half-open [since, until). A movement exactly at since is IN.
A movement exactly at until is OUT. Its redemption is outside the candidate set too, so the period stays available.
A movement before the window contributes nothing.
THE reason the window follows the movement. A reversal posted this period against a redemption verified last period is this period's money movement, and the period can end net negative.

The midnight case. A redemption verified inside the window whose fee row posted just after it: the fee row proves completeness across ALL dates while contributing nothing to this window's gross. Windowing the completeness SEARCH would manufacture an unavailable here.

A genuine success verified BEFORE the window with no fee row at all. It is a real gap, and it is not this period's gap: windowing the CANDIDATE SET on redeemed_at is what keeps one old failure from blanking every report forever.
A scoped call must match the operator's actual scope. The out-of-scope merchant's fee and its missing fee are both invisible.
A live node with no merchants is a real state, not a reason to widen. Empty scope is available zeros — and must never fall back to global.

deduct_success_fee_or_record_arrears will write a fee against a pending redemption if service_role asks it to. A fee may only be counted against a redemption the counter actually verified, and readLedgerFeeTotals builds its genuine set with status = success.

NaN is a valid numeric. PostgreSQL orders it ABOVE every finite value, so `> 0` accepts it and `<= 0` does not catch it, and SUM propagates it — without an explicit rejection the figure would be NaN with invalid_rows 0 and available true.

`infinity` is a valid timestamptz sorting above every bound, so SQL would include it while Date.parse('infinity') is NaN and TypeScript already calls it unknown. Both must refuse it or the two contracts answer differently on the same row.

An August redemption and a valid August fee, followed by a wrong-signed reversal in September. The reversal cannot enter August's totals and cannot prove August's completeness, so it has no bearing on August — it is invalid in its own window, not in this one. Invalidating it here would blank the August report forever.

An in-window redemption with a valid in-window fee AND a second, malformed gross row outside the window. The valid row already answered the completeness question, so the malformed one has no bearing on this period — and invalidating it would blank the period permanently, because a link to a candidate never ages out.

A synthetic movement sitting BESIDE a real one on the same genuine redemption. The demo row is well-formed and correctly signed, so nothing but its own is_demo tag distinguishes it — without that filter it adds KES 70 of invented revenue to a real figure. D188's lesson is that redemptions.is_demo is not a discriminator because claim_deal never sets it, which is a reason to add the parent join, not a reason to ignore a tag the seed scripts do set deliberately.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: FeeLedgerRow carries no is_demo and readLedgerFeeTotals does not select it, so aggregateLedgerFees counts a synthetic movement as genuine. B2b must add the column to the row type, the select, and the aggregator's drop rule.

cases.description: A correctly-signed fee_reversal inserted straight into the ledger, with no fee_reversals audit row behind it. No wallet was credited and no admin approved anything, yet every other test passes it — so it would subtract from net and read as money returned.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees sees only merchant_transactions rows, so it cannot corroborate a reversal against fee_reversals at all. B2b must either have readLedgerFeeTotals join the audit table or carry a corroborated flag on the row.

cases.description: A genuine reversal with its audit row, plus a SECOND fee_reversal ledger row on the same redemption and no audit row of its own. Corroborating by redemption alone would let the second row borrow the first row's audit trail and double the money returned.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees sees only merchant_transactions rows and cannot corroborate a reversal against fee_reversals at all. B2b must join the audit table in readLedgerFeeTotals or carry a corroborated flag on the row.

cases.description: The audit row points at the right ledger row but records a different amount. The ledger says KES 70 was returned and the approval says KES 30 — one of them is wrong and nothing here can tell which, so the figure is not established.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: Same gap: aggregateLedgerFees cannot see fee_reversals, so it cannot notice the approval disagreeing with the ledger. B2b must join the audit table or carry a corroborated flag.

cases.description: A reversal and a matching audit row, but approver_user_id is NULL. reverse_success_fee raises unless the approver's role is admin, so a genuine audit row always names one — and the column is nullable, so an approver-less row is representable and satisfies every other part of corroboration.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees cannot see fee_reversals at all, so it cannot notice a missing approver. B2b must join the audit table in readLedgerFeeTotals or carry a corroborated flag on the row.

cases.description: A correctly-signed success_fee of KES 70 against a redemption whose success_fee_charged is 30. deduct_success_fee_or_record_arrears writes the redemption's own snapshot and pins it to the canonical config fee, and nothing updates that snapshot afterwards — so this row was not written by the money path, and counting it reports revenue nobody billed.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: GenuineFeeRedemption carries success_fee_charged but aggregateLedgerFees never compares it to the ledger amount — it deliberately reads the stored ledger value instead. B2b must decide whether the snapshot is a corroborating check or whether the two implementations differ here on purpose.

cases.description: A redemption naming merchant m1 against merchant m2's deal. claim_deal always copies the deal's merchant into the redemption, so the two parents disagreeing is the cross-merchant corruption one level up — and it would attribute m2's supply to m1.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: The D188 join in readLedgerFeeTotals confirms both parents are non-demo but never compares them to each other, and FeeLedgerRow carries neither. B2b must add the comparison to the reader.

cases.description: A fee written while the redemption was still pending, which later became successful. verify_redemption sets redeemed_at and writes the fee in one transaction, so a fee can never predate its own verification — without this rule the later status transition retroactively legitimises the earlier row.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: GenuineFeeRedemption carries no redeemed_at, so aggregateLedgerFees cannot compare a movement to its verification. B2b must add it to the row type and the reader's select.

cases.description: Two well-formed success_fee rows against one redemption: same merchant, same snapshot, both after verification. Every row is individually valid and the sum reports KES 60 for a KES 30 fee. verify_redemption writes exactly one, but deduct_success_fee_or_record_arrears takes a caller-supplied reference id, so a retry or a direct call produces this.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees sums each row independently and has no notion of a redemption's other fee rows. B2b must add the sibling comparison.

cases.description: A corroborated reversal dated before its redemption was verified. reverse_success_fee refuses a redemption that is not already success, so a reversal cannot predate verification any more than a fee can.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: GenuineFeeRedemption carries no redeemed_at, so aggregateLedgerFees cannot compare any movement to its verification. B2b must add it to the row type and the reader's select.

cases.description: An in-window reversal, fully corroborated, against an older redemption that was never billed at all. reverse_success_fee raises no_fee_to_reverse for exactly this, so the shape is fabricated — and because the redemption is outside the candidate window, nothing else here would have noticed. It would report money returned for a fee that was never charged.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees has no notion of a redemption's other rows, so it cannot tell a reversal has no fee behind it. B2b must add the sibling comparison.

cases.description: One merchant's wallet debit pointing at another merchant's redemption. Nothing in the schema enforces equality and the fee RPC takes a caller-supplied reference id, so it is representable. Attributing it to either merchant is a guess, so it is surfaced instead — and it is visible from BOTH scopes rather than invisible from one.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: FeeLedgerRow carries no merchant_id, so aggregateLedgerFees cannot see the mismatch at all. B2b must add it to the row type and to readLedgerFeeTotals' select.

cases.description: The same corrupt row seen from the OTHER side: the merchant whose wallet was actually debited. Scoping only on the redemption's merchant would make this row invisible here, so the debited merchant's report would read available and complete while its wallet moved.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: FeeLedgerRow carries no merchant_id, so aggregateLedgerFees cannot see the mismatch from either side. B2b must add it to the row type and to readLedgerFeeTotals' select.

cases.description: The completeness search spans all dates, so a malformed row would otherwise buy an available:true with nothing behind it. A zero, wrong-signed or cross-merchant row is not a fee, whatever its date.
cases.notYetInTypeScript: aggregateLedgerFees adds a gross row to `billed` BEFORE testing its polarity, so a malformed out-of-window row still satisfies its completeness check. B2b must move that test ahead of the billed.add.
